title: The Alarm and the Hidden Sins
sum: A voice cries to God, a woman's in Swete's Greek and most naturally Jerusalem's, as war suddenly breaks out. She expected God to answer, because she thought herself full of righteousness: she was prosperous and rich in children. Then she learns the truth. Her children's wealth and glory had spread to the ends of the earth, they had been lifted to the stars and thought they could never fall, and in their good fortune they grew insolent. Their sins were hidden, even from her, and they were worse than the nations': they profaned the Lord's holy things.

The short poem is an overture to the whole book. It names the themes the next psalms develop: war, secret sin, pride before a fall, and the defiled sanctuary. It has no heading in Swete's text (see the note on 1:1).
readings: Read as history

Most readers place the poem in 63 BC, when Pompey's army came to Judea. The prosperity of 1:4-5 fits the last Hasmonean kings, who, Josephus says, had raised the nation "so high" before Pompey confined it to its own borders (Antiquities 14.4.4).
Read as a confession

The speaker is not a neutral reporter. She thought she was righteous (1:2-3) and discovers she did not know her own children (1:7). The poem teaches its hearers to look for the cause of disaster at home first, as the prophets did.

views.H: Gray (1913) read the alarm of war as the distress that struck the whole nation, the righteous and the sinners alike, at the coming of the foreign army. Whether the speaker is Jerusalem depends on the feminine form in 1:3, which only manuscripts l and r have; this site reads her as the city, but Gray does not say so.
views.J: The sins of the rich and powerful are hidden and religious: they profane "the Lord's holy things" (1:8). That points at the priestly rulers of Jerusalem, not at ordinary Jews.
views.P: The poem uses the patterns of the biblical laments: the cry in distress (Psalm 120:1), the proud who rise to the stars and fall (Isaiah 14:13-15; Obadiah 1:4), and Jerusalem as a mother of children (Isaiah 54:1).
views.C: Like the whole book, this psalm was never part of any church's Bible. Swete notes that the Psalms of Solomon "at one time followed the New Testament in the Codex Alexandrinus" and survive in later Greek manuscripts of the Wisdom books (Swete, vol. III, introduction).

echoes: Isaiah 1:21; Isaiah 14:12–15; Obadiah 1:3–4; Isaiah 54:1; Lamentations 1:1; 2 Kings 21:9; Ezekiel 16:47

settings.what: Jerusalem's cry when war breaks out
settings.by: the poet, speaking perhaps as Jerusalem (the feminine "many" of 1:3 in manuscripts l and r)
settings.to: God, overheard by the devout who used the collection
settings.when: the sudden coming of war, most likely Pompey's march on Jerusalem in 63 BC
settings.why: to confess that the city's disaster had a cause inside it: the hidden sins of its powerful children. The hearers are taught to stop trusting their own righteousness (1:2-3) before they ask God to act.
settings.readers: The first hearers were the devout of Jerusalem who used these psalms, most likely in the years after Pompey took the city in 63 BC, when the sudden alarm of 1:1 was a memory they shared. Gray (1913) thought most of the psalms were written soon after 63 BC. The psalms were written in Hebrew, which Gray (1913) called "now generally admitted," and survive in Greek. Ryle and James argued from the Greek's style and its links with Baruch that the translation was made before AD 70; Viteau reached the same date from the Greek, although he rejects the view, which Ryle and James accept, that Baruch depends on Psalm 11 (Gray). The Hebrew is lost.
views: Gray (1913) dated most of the psalms soon after Pompey's invasion of 63 BC and read Psalms 2 and 8 against his campaign; he wrote that "the majority of recent scholars" found the allusions to outside events decisive.
Frankenberg read the conqueror of the collection as Antiochus IV in the 160s BC, as Gray reports.

title: The Dragon on the Shore of Egypt
sum: An arrogant sinner batters down Jerusalem's walls with a ram, and foreign soldiers climb God's altar in their sandals. The poet does not blame God: Jerusalem's sons had already defiled the holy things, and her daughters had defiled themselves. Jerusalem herself is pictured as a queen dragged from her throne, her robes traded for sackcloth and her crown for a rope.

Then the poet prays: enough, Lord; the nations have gone too far, out of greed, not zeal. Do not wait to punish the dragon. And God answers. The poet sees the proud conqueror stabbed on the mountains of Egypt, his body tossed on the waves, unburied, because he forgot that he was only a man. The psalm ends with a warning to the great ones of the earth and a blessing on those who fear God.
readings: Read as history

Nearly every detail fits Pompey: the battering rams of 63 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 14.4.2), the soldiers in the Temple (Histories of Tacitus 5:9), and his murder in 48 BC near Mount Casius, on the coast of Egypt (Cassius Dio 42.5; Plutarch, Pompey 79-80). Gray (1913) found it "difficult to avoid the conclusion" that the conqueror and Pompey are one person, and dated the psalm soon after 48 BC.
Read as theology

The psalm holds two things together. God sent the conqueror to punish his own people (2:3-8, 2:16-19), and God judged the conqueror for his pride (2:25-35). The poet answers suffering not by doubting God but by declaring him in the right (2:16).

views.H: Gray (1913) weighed the identification with Pompey against Frankenberg's with Antiochus IV and found Pompey the only figure who fits all the details, above all the death in Egypt. He noted two differences from the histories: the psalm says nothing of Pompey entering the Holy of Holies, the scandal Josephus and Tacitus record, and it speaks of soldiers trampling the altar, which they do not. Gray also notes that Cheyne (in the Hibbert Journal, 1910) rejected the identification of the dragon with Pompey.
views.J: The psalm reads the Roman conquest the way Lamentations reads the Babylonian one: the defiled sanctuary, the mourning city, the cry "enough" (2:24). Its quarrel is with Jerusalem's leaders, who profaned the gifts, and with the Gentiles, who overstepped.
views.N: The New Testament writers lived under the order Pompey founded: Judea paying tribute to Rome. The psalm's picture of a proud ruler struck down for forgetting he was mortal returns in Acts 12:21-23, and its dragon is a forerunner of the image Revelation 12-13 applies to Satan and the beast.
views.P: The poem borrows the biblical Psalms' forms in turn: lament (2:1-15), declaration that God is just (2:16-19), plea (2:24-29), report of the answer (2:30-35), and a call to the kings like Psalm 2:10-11 (2:36). The dragon recalls the sea monster of Psalm 74:13-14 and the Greek of Jeremiah 51:34.
views.C: The Psalms of Solomon "passed with many other Jewish writings into Christian use," Gray (1913) wrote, classed sometimes with the apocrypha and sometimes with the disputed books, but "their influence on Christian literature was neither very extensive nor intense." For modern readers of every church the psalm is a historical witness, not Scripture: a dated Jewish response to Rome's arrival.

deep.h: The capture of Jerusalem in 63 BC
deep.b: Josephus tells the story twice (Antiquities 14.3-4 and Jewish War 1.6-7, Whiston's translation). The Hasmonean brothers Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II were fighting over the throne and both appealed to Pompey, then campaigning in Syria (Josephus, Antiquities 14.3.1-2). Aristobulus defied him. At Jerusalem the people divided: the party of Hyrcanus opened the city and the palace to Pompey, while Aristobulus's party seized the Temple and cut the bridge. Pompey raised a bank on the north side, working on the Sabbaths, when the defenders would not attack, and brought battering rams from Tyre. In the third month a great tower fell. Twelve thousand Jews died, many at the hands of the other faction. Pompey went into the sanctuary, but, Josephus says, touched none of its treasure; the next day he had the Temple cleansed and restored Hyrcanus as high priest. Cassius Dio, more than a century later, says the defenders were taken on "the day of Saturn" and "all the wealth was plundered" (37.16).

deep.h: The death of Pompey in 48 BC
deep.b:
Fifteen years later Pompey lost the civil war to Julius Caesar and fled by sea to Egypt, where the young king Ptolemy was camped at Pelusium. The king's advisers decided to kill him. Plutarch says that as the small boat carrying Pompey neared the shore, and he took his freedman Philip's hand to rise, his former officer Septimius ran him through from behind, the others stabbed him, and he covered his face with his toga. They cut off his head and threw his body out of the boat; his freedman Philip later burned it on the planks of an old fishing boat (Pompey 77-80). Cassius Dio adds that he died "near Mount Casius," on the anniversary of one of his triumphs, and that the man who had "subdued the entire Roman sea ... perished on it" (42.5).

The psalm's details match closely: stabbed, on the coast of Egypt by the mountain, despised, the body exposed, no proper burial, the boast of being "lord of land and sea." Gray (1913) noted that the psalm's "tossed about on the waves," the reading he took as correct, is further from the literal truth than h's "destroyed" (see the variant at 2:31).

deep.title: Claude's theory: "God is great" as an answer to "Pompey the Great"
deep.b: Gray (1913) wrote in a note that in 2:33 "God, not Pompey, is 'Magnus'." It may go further: the whole of 2:32-36 may be built on the surname. The conqueror is called less than "the least" (2:30), God is "great, mighty in his great strength" (2:33), and the kings are told to see the judgment of the "great king" (2:36). If the psalm was first read soon after 48 BC, when Pompey's title was famous throughout the Roman world, the play on "great" would have been obvious. This is a reading of the Greek; the Hebrew words behind it are lost, so the wordplay cannot be checked in the original.

echoes: Lamentations 1:1–10; Lamentations 2:1; Isaiah 3:24; Isaiah 10:5–15; Jeremiah 51:34; Ezekiel 28:2; Ezekiel 29:3–5; Psalm 2:10–11; Psalm 74:13–14; Psalm 79:1–3; Acts 12:21–23; Revelation 12:9; Baruch 5:1–2; Histories of Tacitus 5:9

settings.what: A lament for Jerusalem and a song of God's justice on her conqueror
settings.by: the poet, speaking for the devout ("I" in 2:15-16, 2:24, 2:30)
settings.to: God (2:1-35), then the great ones of the earth (2:36) and those who fear the Lord (2:37)
settings.when: after Pompey's capture of Jerusalem (63 BC) and, by 2:30-31, soon after his death in Egypt (48 BC)
settings.why: to explain the disaster as God's just punishment of Jerusalem's sins, to pray that God would stop the nations' cruelty, and to celebrate the conqueror's shameful end as God's answer. It taught the devout to keep blessing God (2:37) while the city lay humbled.
settings.readers: The first hearers were devout Jews who had lived through the siege of 63 BC and the trampling of the altar, and had just heard of Pompey's murder in Egypt. If the death in 2:30-31 is Pompey's, the psalm was written after, and probably soon after, 48 BC (Gray, 1913). For them the conqueror's end was fresh news and an answer to prayer.
views: Gray (1913): the death in 2:30-31 is Pompey's, so the psalm was written after, and probably soon after, 48 BC.
Frankenberg, identifying the conqueror with Antiochus IV, had to treat 2:30-35 as a prophecy that was never fulfilled, as Gray reports.

title: The Righteous Rise, the Sinner Falls
sum: The poet wakes his own soul to praise. Then he draws two portraits. The righteous person remembers God, accepts his discipline, and when he stumbles, admits God is right and watches for help. He searches his house for hidden wrongs and atones for sins done in ignorance by fasting. The sinner stumbles too, but he curses the day he was born and piles sin on sin.

The endings differ forever. The sinner falls and "will not rise"; he will not be remembered when God visits the righteous. Those who fear the Lord "will rise to eternal life," a life in the Lord's light that will never end.
readings: Read as wisdom
The psalm is a wisdom poem like Psalm 1 or Psalm 37: two ways of life, two ends. Its point is not that the righteous never fail, but that they respond to failure by turning to God.
Read as a witness to resurrection hope

Written before Jesus, the psalm states plainly that the righteous will rise to eternal life (3:16). Of the sinner it says "he will not rise" (3:13). If that means he will not rise from the dead, the psalm differs from Daniel 12:2, where some wake "to shame"; since the line follows "He fell," it may instead mean that he never recovers from his fall (see the note on 3:13).

views.H: Gray (1913) saw in the book's firm belief in a future life a mark of the Pharisees, whom the New Testament and Josephus describe as holding it. Josephus's own account (Jewish War 2.8.14) says the Pharisees held that the souls of good men only are removed into other bodies, while the souls of bad men suffer eternal punishment. That is not the same picture as the psalm's righteous who "will rise to eternal life" (3:16): Josephus speaks of souls passing into new bodies, the psalm of a rising.
views.J: The righteous man's private piety is striking: daily searching of his home for sin (3:8), and fasting to atone for sins of ignorance (3:9), with no Temple sacrifice mentioned. Gray noted the devout's careful concern about sins of ignorance.
views.N: Jesus speaks of "the resurrection of the righteous" (Luke 14:14), and "eternal life" is the Gospels' term for the life of the age to come (John 5:24). But Paul in Acts speaks of a resurrection "of the righteous and the unrighteous alike" (Acts 24:15), and John 5:28-29 of two resurrections. The site's note on Luke 20:35 cites this psalm for the view that only the righteous rise.
views.P: The opening is a self-address like Psalm 103:1 and Psalm 57:8; the contrast of the two ways is the shape of Psalm 1.

deep.h: Compared with the Bible: who rises?
deep.b: The 66 books speak of resurrection in different ways. Daniel 12:2 says "Some will wake to life without end, and some to shame" (Daniel 12:2): both groups rise. Jesus in John 5:28-29 and Paul in Acts 24:15 speak of a resurrection of the righteous and the unrighteous. The psalm agrees with them that the righteous rise to eternal life, and, if "he will not rise" (3:13) means rising from the dead, goes its own way about the sinner. Christians who read the psalm as history, not Scripture, can take it as evidence of how widely the hope of resurrection had spread among devout Jews before Jesus, and of the questions it still left open.

echoes: Psalm 1; Psalm 37:24; Proverbs 3:11–12; Proverbs 24:16; Job 3:3; Jeremiah 20:14; Daniel 12:2; Luke 14:14; John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15; Hebrews 12:5–11; 2 Maccabees 7:9

settings.what: A wisdom psalm on the righteous and the sinner
settings.by: the poet, first speaking to his own soul (3:1-2)
settings.to: his own soul, then the community of the devout who sing it
settings.when: not tied to an event; Gray (1913) took the collection as the work of one generation, in the middle of the first century BC
settings.why: to rouse the devout to praise, to show them how a righteous person handles failure and suffering, and to assure them that their end, eternal life, is different from the sinner's.
settings.readers: The first hearers were the devout who sang the collection, people who fasted for sins of ignorance and accepted suffering as God's discipline. The psalm names no event. Gray (1913) took the collection as the work of one generation in the middle of the first century BC, so these hearers lived under the last Hasmoneans or under Rome.

title: The Hypocrite in the Council
sum: The poet confronts an unholy man who sits in the devout council. In public he is severe, quick to condemn sinners; in private he chases every woman, lies under oath, and slips into houses as a friend to ruin them. He tells himself that no one sees and no one judges.

The poet answers with a long curse: may God expose him, may his life be poverty and sleeplessness, his old age lonely, and his body left for the beasts and the ravens. The psalm ends by blessing those who fear the Lord in innocence and asking God's mercy on all who love him.
readings: Read as party conflict

Gray (1913) took the people-pleasers to be the Sadducean leaders of Jerusalem, and the devout to be Pharisees; Wellhausen named Alexander Jannaeus, Ryle and James Aristobulus II as the unholy man. The harsh judging of 4:2 recalls Josephus's description of the Sadducees (Antiquities 20.9.1).
Read as a portrait of hypocrisy
The psalm names no party. Its target is a type: the religious leader who plays to the crowd and lives a double life. Read this way, it warns every community, including the one that sang it.

views.H: Ryle and James argued that Psalms 4 and 12, which denounce the sinners but do not yet see them punished, may be the earliest in the collection, perhaps before Pompey (Gray, 1913). The heading's word "conversation" (4:0) fits a poem that begins by speaking to its target.
views.J: The poem shows a quarrel inside Jewish leadership, carried on in the language of the Law: false oaths, adultery, unjust judgment, hypocrisy. Gray thought the evidence pointed to Pharisees against Sadducees. The other proposals, a group like the Essenes or a devout circle that cannot be named, are weighed in the introduction to the book; this psalm's evidence is general enough to fit more than one group.
views.N: Jesus' charges against some scribes and Pharisees are close in kind: hypocrisy and lawlessness (Matthew 23:28), heavy burdens for others (Matthew 23:4), houses of widows eaten up behind long prayers (Mark 12:40). The word "people-pleasers" reappears in Ephesians 6:6 and Colossians 3:22.
views.P: The curse of 4:16-22 is in the form of the biblical cursing psalms (Psalm 109:6-19), and 4:21 takes up the Greek of Psalm 52:6 (Psalm 53:5 in English Bibles): "God scattered the bones of people-pleasers."

echoes: Psalm 10:11; Psalm 53:5; Psalm 109:6–19; Job 24:15; Proverbs 30:17; Deuteronomy 13:9; Deuteronomy 28:19; John 8:7; Matthew 23:4; Matthew 23:28; Mark 12:40; Ephesians 6:6; Colossians 3:22

settings.what: A denunciation of a hypocrite and a curse on him
settings.by: the poet, for the devout ("us" in 4:27)
settings.to: the unholy man himself (4:1), then God (4:16-29)
settings.when: a time when the sinners still held power and sat in the devout council; Ryle and James thought before Pompey, Wellhausen in the reign of Alexander Jannaeus (Gray, 1913)
settings.why: to expose a respected leader as a hypocrite before the community, to hand his punishment over to God in prayer, and to keep the devout from being taken in by his smiles (4:6, 4:25).
settings.readers: The first hearers sat in the same council as the man the psalm attacks, while he and his kind still held power and had not been punished. Ryle and James argued that Psalms 4 and 12, where the sinners are denounced but not yet punished and no Gentile intervention is in view, may be the earliest of the collection, written before Pompey's invasion of 63 BC; Wellhausen placed Psalm 4 in the reign of Alexander Jannaeus (103-78 BC), which Gray (1913) called uncertain. On either view the hearers knew the man.
views: Gray (1913): the sinners are Sadducees and the devout Pharisees; compare Josephus, Antiquities 20.9.1.
Gray (1913) gives Wellhausen's view that the unholy man is Alexander Jannaeus, and Ryle and James's that he is Aristobulus II.

title: God Feeds the Poor
sum: A poor man praises God among those who know his judgments. God is the refuge of the poor; no one can take anything that God does not give, and each person's share is weighed out by him. When we are in trouble we will call, and even if God does not answer at once, we will keep coming. God feeds the birds and the fish, sends rain on the desert, and feeds kings and peoples. Who else is the hope of the poor?

People are stingy with kindness and put things off; God's gift is rich. Happy is the one God gives just enough: too much leads to sin, and a modest share with righteousness is blessing. God's kindness rests on Israel, and he is our king.
readings: Read as a prayer of the poor
The psalm is the voice of the devout poor (5:2), who trust God for daily bread. Its argument from God's care for animals is the argument of Matthew 6:26.
Read as wisdom on wealth
Verses 18-20 are a little treatise on enough. They agree with Proverbs 30:8-9 and 1 Timothy 6:6-8, and they answer Psalm 1's picture of the rich who grew insolent in their good times (1:6).

views.J: Gray (1913) saw in the book's "poor" the devout themselves, largely people of small means (compare 10:7), and found here the idea, later typical of the Pharisees in Josephus's account, that God fixes each person's lot while people remain responsible (5:4-6; Josephus, Jewish War 2.8.14).
views.N: "Blessed are the poor" (Luke 6:20), the birds the Father feeds (Matthew 6:26), and the strong man whose goods cannot be taken (Mark 3:27) all have echoes here.
views.P: The psalm is built from Psalms 104 and 145: God's open hand (Psalm 145:16), the creatures that wait on him (Psalm 104:27), and the closing confession of God as king (Psalm 145:1).

echoes: Psalm 104:10–28; Psalm 145:15–16; Psalm 147:9; Proverbs 30:8–9; Isaiah 49:24; Matthew 6:26; Mark 3:27; Luke 6:20; 1 Timothy 6:6–8

settings.what: A poor man's hymn of trust
settings.by: the poet, "I" who is poor and hungry (5:10), joined by "we" (5:7-9)
settings.to: God, "among those who know your righteous judgments" (5:1): the gathered devout
settings.when: a time of trouble and need (5:7-8); no event is named
settings.why: to keep the devout poor praying even when God seems slow (5:9), and to teach contentment with God's measure (5:18-20) instead of envy of the rich.
settings.readers: The first hearers were the poor among the devout, people who knew hunger and need (5:7-10) and lived beside richer neighbors. The psalm names no event; on Gray's view of the collection (1913) they lived in the middle of the first century BC.

title: Ready to Call on the Lord
sum: A short psalm of trust. Happy is the man whose heart is ready to call on the Lord's name: he will be saved, his paths are made straight, bad dreams and dangerous waters do not frighten him. He rises from sleep blessing God, sings with a steady heart, and prays for his household. The Lord hears all who fear him and grants what they hope for.
readings: Read as a portrait
The psalm is a picture of the devout man at prayer, morning and night, in the home. It complements the righteous man of Psalm 3.
Read with Joel
"Call on the name" and "he will be saved" (6:1-2) are the words of Joel 2:32, which Peter and Paul apply to calling on Jesus (Acts 2:21; Romans 10:13).

views.N: The pairing of calling on the Lord's name with being saved is the pattern of Joel 2:32 that Romans 10:13 quotes. The psalm shows the promise being prayed in Jewish homes before the New Testament applied it to Jesus.
views.P: The language is that of Psalms 57:7 (the ready or firm heart, in the Greek), 91:5 (no fear at night) and 3:5 (lying down and rising in God's care).

echoes: Joel 2:32; Romans 10:13; Psalm 57:7; Psalm 91:5; Psalm 3:5; Isaiah 43:2; Job 1:5

settings.to: the devout who sing it, about the man who calls on God
settings.when: not tied to an event; the heading is "In hope"
settings.why: to hold up the praying man as the model for every devout household, and to assure the hearers that God hears those who fear him.
settings.readers: The first hearers were devout households whose head, like the man of the psalm, blessed God on waking and prayed for the whole house (6:6-7), and who wanted assurance that God hears. The psalm names no event; on Gray's view of the collection (1913) they lived in the middle of the first century BC.

title: Do Not Take Your Tent from Us
sum: The devout beg God not to leave them: if he moves his tent away, their enemies will attack and trample his holy inheritance. Let God discipline them himself, as he wills, but never hand them over to the nations. Even if he sends death, it obeys his orders, and he is merciful. While his name dwells among them they will find mercy; no nation will overpower them. They accept his yoke and his whip forever, and wait for the day he promised the house of Jacob.
readings: Read before the disaster
The psalm may be a prayer before the sanctuary fell, asking God to keep the foreigners out (7:2).
Read after the disaster
Or it may be a prayer from the ruins: the devout accept that God's discipline came, and ask only that it come from God's own hand, not the nations'.

views.H: Gray (1913) thought the enemies of 7:1 are foreigners, and that the heading "Of turning" (7:0) most likely means God's restoring of his people (7:9).
views.J: The poem's center is God's name "dwelling" (7:5) among his people, the language of Deuteronomy 12:11 and 1 Kings 8:29. Its fear is the fear of Ezekiel 10-11: that the presence would leave the Temple.
views.N: John uses the same tent-dwelling verb: the Word "pitched his tent among us" (John 1:14). Jesus offers his own yoke (Matthew 11:29-30), and Hebrews 12:5-11 reads suffering as a father's discipline.
views.P: The plea "do not hand us over to the nations" follows David's choice in 2 Samuel 24:14 and the laments' "correct me, but not in your anger" (Jeremiah 10:24; Psalm 6:1).

echoes: 2 Samuel 24:13–15; Jeremiah 10:24; Psalm 6:1; Psalm 69:4; Ezekiel 10:18–19; John 1:14; Lamentations 3:27; Hebrews 12:5–11; Matthew 11:29–30

settings.what: A community prayer for God's presence
settings.when: under threat from foreign enemies; whether before or after the fall of the sanctuary in 63 BC the poem does not say
settings.why: to ask that God stay among his people, to accept his discipline while refusing to be handed over to the nations, and to hold God to the day he promised.
settings.readers: The first hearers were a community that feared foreign enemies and the loss of God's presence among them. Whether they sang it before the sanctuary fell in 63 BC or after, the poem does not say; Gray (1913) took the collection as the work of one generation in the middle of the first century BC.

title: The War at Jerusalem
sum: The poet hears the trumpet of war and the roar of an army sweeping toward Jerusalem, and his body gives way. He thought the city was righteous; then God shows him its hidden sins: incest, adultery, robbing the sanctuary, coming to the altar unclean and treating the sacrifices like ordinary meat. So God made Jerusalem's leaders drunk with a spirit of going astray.

God brought the one from the far end of the earth. The rulers welcomed him with joy, smoothed the roads and opened the gates. He came in like a father, then seized the towers, killed the leaders, poured out blood like water and led sons and daughters away. God was shown to be right; the devout were like lambs among the nations. The psalm ends with a long prayer: turn your mercy to us, gather the scattered of Israel, do not let the nations swallow us. We will not leave you.
readings: Read as history

This is the book's fullest account of the conquest. Gray (1913) matched it step by step with Josephus: Aristobulus's gift and surrender of his fortresses (Antiquities 14.3), the party of Hyrcanus opening the city (14.4.2), the siege of the Temple, the executions and the twelve thousand dead (14.4.2-4; Jewish War 1.7.5-6), and the captives taken to Rome (14.4.5).
Read as theodicy
The poet's question is God's justice. His answer is in two parts: God was right to judge Jerusalem (8:7-26), and he will still be faithful to the devout and to scattered Israel (8:27-40).

views.H: Gray (1913) read 8:16-24 as Pompey's campaign, and mentioned the older comparison with Antiochus IV, whose party opened Jerusalem's gates to him (Josephus, Antiquities 12.5.3). The welcome by "the rulers of the land" (8:18) fits Hyrcanus's party; the seizure of the towers (8:21) fits the siege of the Temple held by Aristobulus's men.
views.J: The sins listed are priestly sins: robbing the sanctuary and eating sacrifices in uncleanness (8:12-13). Gray took them as charges against the Temple leadership by its opponents, and warned that partisan charges should not be read too literally.
views.N: The cup of unmixed wine (8:15) is the image of Revelation 14:10, and the line about a spirit of going astray echoes, as 2 Thessalonians 2:11 also does, the language of God sending delusion. The prayer to gather the dispersion (8:34) is the hope behind the New Testament's "Dispersion" (James 1:1).
views.P: The psalm moves through the stages of the biblical community laments (Psalm 79; Psalm 80): the disaster, confession that God is just, and plea for mercy and gathering.
views.C: Christian book lists of the early Middle Ages name the collection: the Synopsis ascribed to Athanasius puts the Psalms of Solomon among the disputed books, and Nicephorus of Constantinople (patriarch 806-814) lists them between Ecclesiastes and Esther (Gray, 1913). No church received them into its Bible.

deep.b:
Gray (1913) set the psalm beside Josephus, verse by verse. 8:16-17: the conqueror comes "from the far end of the earth," as the Greek of Deuteronomy 28:49 describes a foreign nation. 8:18-19: on Pompey's way south from Damascus, Aristobulus sent him a golden vine worth five hundred talents and later handed over his fortresses (Antiquities 14.3.1, 14.3.4); at Jerusalem, "the others admitted Pompey's army in, and delivered up both the city and the king's palace to him" (14.4.2). 8:21: Aristobulus's party held the Temple until the siege works brought down a tower (14.4.2-4). 8:23: Pompey executed "those that had been the authors of that war" (14.4.4), and twelve thousand Jews died, most, the Jewish War says, "by their own countrymen" (1.7.5). 8:24: Aristobulus and his children were taken to Rome (14.4.5).

The fit is close but poetic. The psalm does not name anyone, and it adds what no history reports: the charges of incest and adultery against Jerusalem's leaders (8:9-11).

echoes: Deuteronomy 28:49; Isaiah 19:14; Isaiah 41:25; Jeremiah 4:19; Jeremiah 25:15–16; Ezekiel 8:7–12; Ezekiel 22:10–11; Leviticus 15:31; Psalm 79; Psalm 80; Revelation 14:10; 2 Thessalonians 2:11; James 1:1; Wisdom of Solomon 12:22

settings.what: A lament over the capture of Jerusalem and a prayer for mercy and gathering
settings.to: God, with the devout as hearers
settings.when: after Pompey's capture of Jerusalem in 63 BC and the deportation of captives to Rome
settings.why: to make sense of the catastrophe by confessing that God judged the city justly, and to keep the devout praying for mercy, for the return of the scattered, and for God's faithfulness to them and their children (8:39).
settings.readers: The first hearers had seen Jerusalem's rulers welcome Pompey, the Temple besieged, its defenders killed and captives taken to Rome. Gray (1913) matched the psalm's details with Josephus's account of 63 BC, so it was written after those events, most likely soon after.
views: Gray (1913): the welcome, the siege of the Temple, the executions and the captives all match Josephus's account of 63 BC.
An older comparison, with Antiochus IV's capture of Jerusalem, whose party opened the gates to him (Josephus, Antiquities 12.5.3, as Gray reports).
